summary: Reports an official IAB policy position on network management in the Internet, from the second ad hoc review group meeting on June 12, 1989. The results of the first such meeting appeared in RFC 1052.

eli5.summary: A group of experts met to decide how the Internet should keep an eye on its own machines. This is their report and advice.

subtitle: The 1989 follow-up review that loosened the link between SNMP and CMOT and their shared MIB.

tldr.problem: RFC 1052 had tied SNMP and CMOT to one common MIB and SMI. In practice that appeared to have stifled exploration of new variables and functions in operating networks.
tldr.mechanism: The second ad hoc review, on June 12, 1989, recommended letting SNMP and CMOT explore new variables and possibly non-overlapping SMI definitions independently for 12 months, with unshared variables placed in experimental or private MIB space.
tldr.outcome: The IAB approved the report and adopted its recommendations on July 11-13, 1989. It also called for reconvening the review group at 6 month intervals.

today: RFC 1109 is a policy report from August 1989 that follows RFC 1052; the metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the IAB position at that time, not a protocol.

sections.title: Where SNMP, CMOT and the MIB Stood
sections.content:
The first review (RFC 1052) selected two protocols for further work: SNMP and CMOT, the Common Management Information Protocol on TCP. Both then advanced to Draft-Standard/Recommended status (SNMP in RFC 1098, CMOT in RFC 1095). The Internet SMI and MIB had been specified in RFC 1065 and RFC 1066.

The public part of the Internet MIB held roughly 100 mandatory variables. A typical SNMP monitoring system might support 100 to 200 additional objects in private or experimental MIB space. SNMP was in use in a number of networks and had implementations from several vendors, plus freely available versions. For CMOT, no publicly available implementations were reported at the meeting, though vendors were reported to be planning them.

Scaling remained a challenge. Fault monitoring scaled more easily than performance and configuration monitoring, because the former may work on an exception basis while the latter likely needs periodic reporting.
sections.eli5: Two network-checking tools were both approved. One was already used in lots of places, and the other was still waiting for people to build it.

sections.title: Open Problems
sections.content:
The report lists gaps. Neither SNMP nor CMOT covers software downloading, configuration management or user access control, and authenticating the source of management commands and responses was another important area. Defining objects below IP was hard, since IP runs over many media. Information about the transient state of a TCP connection can vanish with its Transmission Control Block.

Research questions included how to relate groups of monitored variables across layers (such as IP over X.25), and how to tell which version of the MIB a monitored system implements. Archiving collected operational data and registering managed objects were also open. The RFC 1052 plan to bind both protocols to one MIB and SMI made switching protocols easier in theory but, in practice, appears to have stifled exploration of new variables and functions.

The review also noted that neither SNMP nor CMIS has any sense of time other than "now", so neither can express historical queries or commands like doing something in 30 minutes. A common API over several protocols stayed open for investigation. NIST was working on objects at layers 3 and 4 and the Internet SMI was found not to be quite a subset of the ISO SMI.
sections.eli5: The experts listed what the tools still could not do, like remembering the past or knowing who is really giving the orders.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
The attendees concluded that the Internet will exist in a pluralistic protocol stack environment, that growth of the common MIB had been impeded by failure to agree on a common extended SMI, that the community must not ignore other groups' work while coping with operational needs, and that without operational experience with OSI management tools no coexistence and transition plan can be specified.

From this they derived five aims: foster real CMOT/CMIP use; extend SNMP as needed for operational reasons; preserve the utility of the first common MIB (RFC 1066); develop experimental and enterprise variables separately and seek to place them in the common MIB; and in a coexisting environment, reach the same variables in a device by more than one protocol.
sections.eli5: They agreed the Internet will keep using many kinds of network languages, so the tools must be able to get along.

sections.title: Recommendations to the IAB
sections.content:
The review recommended that SNMP and CMOT efforts be allowed to explore new variables and possibly non-overlapping SMI definitions independently for the next 12 months. The binding to a common MIB/SMI would be relaxed. Variables that cannot be supported by both protocols belong in the experimental or private parts of the MIB space. The CMOT group should move its MIB and SMI toward the OSI/NIST specifications.

It also urged the IAB to encourage Internet elements that use OSI protocols, to keep up active liaison with NIST on coexistence, and to direct the IETF to restructure its network management efforts accordingly. Finally, the Ad Hoc Review Group should be reconvened at 6 month intervals to see whether the common MIB/SMI can grow again.
sections.eli5: For a year, each tool may try its own new ideas. The experts will meet again every six months to see what can be shared.
